title: Fairness through Causal Awareness
abstract: How do we learn from biased data? Historical datasets often reflect historical prejudices; sensitive or protected attributes may affect the observed treatments and outcomes. Classification algorithms tasked with predicting outcomes accurately from these datasets tend to replicate these biases. We advocate a causal modeling approach to learning from biased data, exploring the relationship between fair classification and intervention. We propose a causal model in which the sensitive attribute confounds both the treatment and the outcome. Building on prior work in deep learning and generative modeling, we describe how to learn the parameters of this causal model from observational data alone, even in the presence of unobserved confounders. We show experimentally that fairness-aware causal modeling provides better estimates of the causal effects between the sensitive attribute, the treatment, and the outcome. We further present evidence that estimating these causal effects can help learn policies that are both more accurate and fair, when presented with a historically biased dataset.

claims.text: FCVAE-2 achieves lower PEHE (2.78 ± 0.06) when estimating the causal effect A -> Y on the IHDP dataset (no features removed) compared to CVAE-A (3.04 ± 0.06) and CFMLP (3.28 ± 0.07).
FCVAE-2 achieves lower policy regret (0.19 ± 0.01) on IHDP data with no features removed compared to CVAE-A (0.21 ± 0.01) and CFMLP (0.37 ± 0.02).

FCVAE-2 achieves a lower treatment policy accuracy gap (0.030 ± 0.001 with 0 features removed, 0.027 ± 0.001 with 1 feature removed) than CVAE-A (0.033 ± 0.001, 0.028 ± 0.001) and CFMLP (0.042 ± 0.002, 0.033 ± 0.002).
Explicitly modeling the sensitive attribute as a confounder allows the model to learn interventional distributions with respect to the sensitive attribute.

limitations.text: Supervised classification paradigms applied to decision-making ignore counterfactual outcomes and replicate past dataset biases.
If there are unobserved confounding factors that cannot be inferred from the observed proxies, the joint distribution cannot be learned and causal effects become unidentifiable.
The framework assumes binary sensitive attributes and binary treatments, which may not represent optimal modeling choices in all practical applications.
Testing for unconfoundedness is difficult and usually requires making further assumptions.

future_work.text: Implementing counterfactual fairness policies by assigning treatments based on inferred outcome distributions under a fixed counterfactual value of sensitive attribute A.
Decomposing A -> Y into direct and indirect effects via mediation analysis of T to support path-specific fairness.
Utilizing causal effect estimations between A, T, and Y to establish bias auditing techniques for historical datasets.
Applying counterfactual predictions of A and T for fair missing data imputation.

methodologies.name: Fair Causal Variational Autoencoder (FCVAE)
methodologies.description: A deep latent-variable model combining structural causal modeling with amortized variational inference to model unobserved confounders and explicitly treat sensitive attributes as confounders affecting treatment and outcome.
conditions: evaluations with 0, 1, or 2 informative proxies removed
